title: Go First 16, 2026
author: Secondary Literacy Commons
summary: This recap of the September Secondary Literacy Commons session distills a month of discussion about what leadership of secondary literacy improvement actually looks like. It opens from Terrie Noland's charge to 'go first' and argues that literacy leadership is not about titles but about modeling and influence. The central tension the group identified is between co-creation and accountability: co-created plans without accountability get ignored, while mandates without co-creation produce compliance that evaporates. The piece then names a quiet belief behind secondary resistance, that older students already know how to read, and argues that only influence, not policy, dislodges it. It closes by distinguishing 'literacy-in-name' from a felt, whole-school belief in the work, positioning data, visible practice, and coherent structures as the bridge between the two. The operational target is school leaders and teachers building a school-wide literacy culture, which places it in Practice & Culture rather than Learning & Curriculum.
points: Co-creation and accountability must be paired: planning that lets teachers push back surfaces resistance early, but leaders must then hold structures in place when results are slow.
The belief that grades 6-12 students already read well enough cannot be mandated away; it shifts only when teachers see respected colleagues and leaders actually doing the practices.
Low secondary literacy proficiency is often tolerated out of affection for students, so leaders must adopt the stance that struggling to read may be how students arrive but not how they leave.
Secondary literacy is a whole-school responsibility, and coherence often means using existing expertise, such as SLPs and MTSS coordinators, rather than buying a new program.
Content-area assessment data showing students struggling most with science and social studies texts moved those teachers from 'literacy-in-name' toward genuine ownership.
quotes: There’s a key theme from Terrie Noland’s contribution to Reading Isn’t Optional that we used to open September’s Secondary Literacy Commons (SLC) session: Go first, be an advocate, be a thought partner for planning and implementation. It’s written as guidance to school leaders. But the group took it as guidance for everyone in this community, whatever role they hold.
Co-creation without top-down accountability produces a well-built plan everyone is free to ignore. Top-down accountability without co-creation produces compliance that ends the day the pressure does.

Letting teachers surface concerns and push back during the planning process isn’t weakness — it is a strategy. The resistance that comes out in a planning meeting is the resistance that doesn’t derail implementation later.

Here is a belief that sits underneath a lot of resistance to supporting literacy in middle and high schools, rarely stated out loud: kids in grades 6–12 already know how to read, so my job is to teach my content area not reading. You cannot mandate your way out of that belief. It doesn’t respond to a new policy or a required training. It responds to influence.

You can require a teacher to sit through a workshop on morphology instruction. You cannot require them to believe it matters for their students. Getting from the former to the latter is the actual work of leadership, and it’s slower and more relational than most systems are built to support.

One of the clearest takeaways from the session’s reading on exemplary high schools was also the most uncomfortable: low levels of proficiency in literacy have been tolerated for too long. That tolerance isn’t usually malicious. It’s often rooted in genuine affection for students and a reluctance to hold them to standards they feel set up to fail.

The mindset shift that effective leadership requires: struggling to read may be how students arrive; it is not how students leave our school. Evidence-based literacy instruction needs to be visible at every grade level, not just in Kindergarten through 3rd grade. Leaders in middle and high school need to expect it, monitor for it, and build the conditions that make it possible.

Leadership doesn’t manufacture belief. But it creates the conditions in which belief becomes possible: the data that makes the problem visible, the training that makes the solution accessible, the structures that make the practice sustainable, and the culture that makes trying something new feel safe.
